newsitem.title: USA: U.S Crude Outlook--Crude supported by arb and heat.
newsitem.headline: U.S Crude Outlook--Crude supported by arb and heat.

text.p: U.S. crude prices this week remain in a defensive posture after recent slides but should find some toe-hold support from bullish heating oil and a tight arbitrage, traders and analysts said Monday.
Domestic light, sweet grade differentials held to their lofty levels early Monday after a brief speculative downturn, protected by refiner demand amid thin supplies.

"LLS (Light Louisiana Sweet/St James) will continue to be strong for a while, a function of the Dated Brent to WTI (West Texas Intermediate) spread which has been persistently tight," said John Saucer, analyst with Smith Barney in Houston.
NYMEX December crude rallied higher to close firmly at $23.59 a barrel Friday, after dropping to $22.47 a barrel.
While managing to stage a recovery on the back of heating oil which was inspired by a fall in inventories and colder weather forecast, a price retreat was seen still on the cards.

"Crude is rather neutral and lows last week will prove significant," Saucer said, adding that although refiners will push incremental barrels for heating oil, there was formidable resistance at 70 cents a gallon for the fuel.
He predicted January crude, which starts trading next week, may be impacted by lesser crude distillation capacity.

"Imports are still up with no decline from the region and the Middle East," said Paulo Nery, senior consultant with The Pace Consultants in Houston, noting the narrow North Sea arbitrage was only a bullish factor for light, sweet crudes.
Domestic grades were expected to trade within established ranges with a flatter backwardation between Dec/Jan chiselling down the value of WTI/Cushing Posting Plus.

Louisiana sweet grades have found sustained support from the closed arbitrage, although increasing pressure on Dated Brent in European markets could pry open the trans-Atlantic import window, traders said.
"Refiners will be doing heavy maintenance work on crude distillation units in the first quarter," Saucer said, noting downtime to be the heaviest in several years.
Many companies had kept scheduled autumn turnarounds to a minimum, to capitalize on bullish petroleum product prices.

Outright crude prices advanced 80 cents late last week on forecasts for a cold snap in the U.S. Northeast, but traders conceded that markets were still in search of a new bottom and looked for a definitive test of underlying support.
"There is no reason to feel the market isn't well-supplied and ready to fall back again," said a Texas cash crude trader.
Heavy sours appeared the most vulnerable due to competing Canadian and Latin American supplies, and extra sales from the U.S. governement's Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR).
Concern over a possible Venezuelan oil workers strike this week lent psychological support, but no evidence of any action early Monday caused sours to languish at weaker levels.

On the West Coast, crude traders said California and Alaskan business could liven up after a month-and-a-half of razor-thin activity. Arco will also ask oil companies to hand in space requests on California's Line 63 early, on November 15, due to the U.S. Thanksgiving Day holiday later this month.
